body: Performance improvements are almost always welcome. I would have to see a PR to properly judge if the additional complexity/maintenance burden is justifiable though.

While the optimization as proposed in the PR is necessary, there's a few alarm bells ringing on my head at the problem here.

> As I can create 100 shared textures per frame

Shared texture creation is not necessarily as free as it might sound. Each shared texture implies quite a lot of allocation and worst of all, a driver call to create an image view. You don't have many guarantees of this driver call taking an amount of time that is reasonable to be per-frame.

I'd like to know what scenario could lead you to needing to do the shared texture creation per frame. Any pattern that leads you to needing allocations per frame is a bit of a red flag and might mean either we have a design problem blocking you from achieving what you need or there's some flaw in the solution.

> I am worried about maintainability and if you would like to support such a use case in the first place.

As I mentioned above, you have to go through a driver creation call, so it's not even necessarily up to us. As far as I'm aware, there's no guarantee for image view creation to be a lightweight enough operation to be run per frame.

@DarioSamo Thanks for your answer.
I implemented an Earth-sized quadtree terrain where each chunk is rendered with the same shader. The shader uses several `Texture2DArray` uniforms (for albedo, normals, etc.) and a layer_index instance uniform (one chunk one layer). Shared textures are created only when a new chunk is generated. These shared textures are the mipmaps of the albedo texture, they are generated on the GPU via a Vulkan texture blit command.

I'm still deciding on the final resolution for the albedo texture, but currently, it’s set to 256x256, which corresponds to 8 mipmap levels plus 1 for the base level. The numbers in my original post are the worst-case scenario: the observer is moving fast at ground level and up to 16 chunks can be created per frame. This results in 144 shared textures created per frame under these conditions.

I plan to cap the maximum depth of the quadtree when the observer is moving rapidly near the ground. There’s no need to generate highly detailed chunks for only a single frame, so this adjustment should reduce the number of shared textures created per frame to a more reasonable level.
